passage:
At break, Preeti was spinning her old wooden top on the cement of the school courtyard, tongue between her teeth. Aadhya walked up with a shiny gadget that beeped and lit up. "Look, my uncle sent it from Dubai." A few children crowded round.
Preeti watched for a moment. "That's nice," she said, and went back to her top. It wobbled, spun long, and she clapped. "Did you see? It went nine counts!" She counted the last wobble out loud.
When the bell rang she tucked the top into her pocket and skipped to class, humming. Aadhya glanced at the crowd, then at Preeti, and wandered over to watch the top.

qa.q: How many counts did Preeti's top spin?
qa.a: Preeti's top spun nine counts.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling as she clapped for her top?
qa.a: Preeti was happy and content. She did not compare her old top with the shiny gadget and enjoyed her own game.

qa.q: What could a teacher or parent do to protect this kind of contentment from peers' possessions?
qa.a: They could notice and enjoy the simple game with Preeti, and talk about what makes a play afternoon good, rather than praise or pity what others have.

qa.q: What might Aadhya have been feeling when wandering over to watch the top?
qa.a: Aadhya may have felt curious and a bit lonely. Showing off the gadget drew a crowd, but the top looked like more fun.

grounding: A child is satisfied with a simple toy and a good afternoon and does not compare it with others' possessions.

passage:
I'm Ramesh, and from my window I can see the empty plot where Neelam plays every afternoon with a plain rubber ball and a stick. She must be nine. Yesterday the boy from the next lane turned up with a bag of new toys and a remote-control car. Neelam looked at the car for a minute, said "Cool," and went back to throwing the ball at the wall. When an advert for a doll house came on at the tea stall's TV, she barely looked up. She was singing while she threw.
I can't know what goes on inside her, but she seemed to have everything she wanted. I wonder how long that lasts once more of the lane starts showing up with new things.

qa.q: What does Neelam play with in the empty plot?
qa.a: Neelam plays with a plain rubber ball and a stick.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling as she went back to throwing the ball after the car arrived?
qa.a: Neelam seemed content and absorbed, singing as she threw, though Ramesh cannot know for sure.

qa.q: What could the adults around Neelam do to keep her contentment strong?
qa.a: They could keep joining her simple games and pay attention to what she enjoys, without pushing purchases or making comparisons.

qa.q: How might the boy from the next lane have felt when Neelam said "Cool" and went back to her game?
qa.a: He may have felt a little let down or puzzled, since he arrived with new toys and did not get the excitement he expected.

grounding: A child is happy with a simple ball and a good afternoon and does not compare, though the contentment is fragile against ads and peers.

passage:
"Kashish, look! It's remote-controlled!" Manjula zoomed a shiny red car across the floor.
"Cool," said Kashish, still folding a paper boat.
"What are you making?"
"A boat. For the puddle outside. It's been raining all day."
"That's just paper."
"Yeah. But watch." Kashish ran to the verandah and set it in the big puddle. It spun and bobbed. Kashish laughed, clapping. "It floats!"
Manjula came to watch. "Mine's better, though."
Kashish paused. For a second, looked at the red car. "Maybe." Then shrugged. "But this one's mine, and it's a good afternoon."
Manjula squatted next to the puddle. "Can you make me one?"
"Sure. Paper boats are the best."

qa.q: What was Kashish making?
qa.a: A paper boat for the puddle outside.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel when the boat floated?
qa.a: Kashish felt happy and delighted, laughing and clapping at the puddle.

qa.q: How could Kashish hold on to that contentment when friends show off new things?
qa.a: Kashish could keep enjoying what's in hand, like the boat, and remember that a good afternoon doesn't depend on having the best toy.

qa.q: How did Manjula's view of the paper boat change?
qa.a: At first Manjula thought it was just paper, but after watching it float, Manjula wanted one too.

grounding: Shows a child satisfied with a simple toy on a good afternoon, briefly tempted by a friend's shinier toy before choosing contentment.

passage:
On Sunday I spent the whole afternoon with Rafiq building a racetrack for marbles out of old cardboard tubes and tape. We made a loop, a jump and a tunnel. When the blue marble made it through the loop, we screamed so loud Amma came to check.
That evening I thought it was the best day of the whole month.
Then on TV there was an ad for a huge plastic racetrack with lights and sounds. Suddenly our tubes looked sad and floppy. I told Amma I wanted it. She asked, "Were you happy this afternoon?" I said yes. She said, "Then nothing about the afternoon changed."
I was still a bit grumpy. But the next day Rafiq and I added a second loop. I'm Shankar, and I think our track is better.

qa.q: What did Shankar and Rafiq build the racetrack from?
qa.a: Old cardboard tubes and tape.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel after seeing the TV ad?
qa.a: Shankar felt dissatisfied and a bit grumpy, as the homemade track suddenly looked sad and floppy.

qa.q: What did Amma's question help Shankar see?
qa.a: That the afternoon had been happy and nothing about it had changed, only the comparison with the ad.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel adding a second loop the next day?
qa.a: Rafiq was probably excited and proud, enjoying the track they built together.

grounding: Shows a child happy with a simple homemade toy until an advertisement makes it seem lacking, showing how fragile contentment is.

passage:
Summer camp note, day three.
Sharmila (8) spent the whole morning with an empty cardboard box. She made it a boat, then a house, then a shop that sold leaves. She hummed the entire time.
At snack time, Jagdish brought out a new handheld game and showed it around. Several children crowded him. Sharmila watched from her box for a while, then asked, "Does it do anything else?" Jagdish shrugged. She went back to her shop, but I noticed she stopped humming.
In the afternoon I invited both of them to build a box city together. Jagdish put his game away after ten minutes. Sharmila was humming again by the end. I'll keep boxes and simple materials out for the rest of the week.

qa.q: What did Sharmila's shop sell?
qa.a: Leaves.

qa.q: What does Sharmila stopping humming suggest?
qa.a: It suggests her contentment wobbled a little, and she may have felt slightly left out or unsure after seeing the new game.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do next, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: They invited both children to build a box city together, which brought Jagdish into simple play and let Sharmila's happiness return.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have felt building the box city?
qa.a: He seemed to enjoy it, since he put his game away after ten minutes.

grounding: Shows a child happy with a simple cardboard box whose contentment wobbles when a peer shows off a new gadget.

passage:
Sunday
Farida's diary. Best afternoon. Abba fixed my old kite with tape and a bit of newspaper, and it flew higher than the water tank. We ate roasted chana on the roof and I didn't want anything else in the world.
Then Pankaj came up with his new remote-control car that lights up. Everybody ran to see it. For a minute my kite felt like rubbish and I wanted to ask Abba for a car too. But then the car's battery died and Pankaj had to go down. My kite was still up there, pulling. I think my afternoon was already good before the car came. I'm keeping the tape for next time.

qa.q: What did Abba use to fix the kite?
qa.a: He used tape and a bit of newspaper.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when Pankaj brought his remote-control car?
qa.a: For a minute Farida felt envious and dissatisfied, as if the kite had turned into rubbish, and wanted a car too.

qa.q: What helped Farida feel content again?
qa.a: Noticing the kite still flying and remembering that the afternoon had been good before the car arrived 🙂

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt when his car's battery died?
qa.a: He probably felt disappointed and a bit embarrassed, having to go down just when everyone was watching.

grounding: Shows a child content with a mended kite and a rooftop afternoon, briefly shaken by a friend's shiny new toy.
